lesson.title: Single-line diagrams: from each source to each load

interactive.brief: The one thing you should see is a load stay lit after you open its usual breaker, because another closed path still joins it to a source, when you tap breakers open and closed on the board.
interactive.title: The switchboard you open and close
interactive.whatAmILookingAt: A short lesson in thirteen small screens. Some screens show an idea and the rest ask you to try it. The main picture is a single-line diagram of a small switchboard, with example values. At the top are three sources. Generator set -G1 feeds through its breaker -Q1. Generator set -G2 feeds through its breaker -Q2. The shore supply feeds through shore breaker -Q3. Below them is the 440 V main board, drawn as a thick busbar in two sections, A on the left and B on the right. -Q1 joins -G1 to section A. -Q2 and -Q3 join -G2 and the shore supply to section B. Between the sections sits bus-tie -Q4, marked N.O. for normally open. Section A feeds three breakers. -Q11 feeds pump -M1. -Q12 feeds transformer -T1, 440 V to 115 V, and a small 115 V board. There, breaker -F1 feeds lighting -E1 and -F2 feeds fan -M4. -Q13 feeds pump -M3. Section B feeds three breakers too. -Q21 feeds pump -M2. -Q22 feeds charger -U1, which turns 440 V AC into 24 V DC for a DC board. Battery -G3 joins that board through isolator -Q5. There -F3 feeds emergency lighting -E3 and -F4 feeds alarm panel -A3. -Q23, marked N.O., is a second feed to pump -M3, from section B. A dashed link between -Q13 and -Q23 is labelled interlocked. A caption under the sheet gives the board as drawn: -G1 and -G2 running, -Q3, -Q4 and -Q23 open, everything else closed. It adds that a single-line diagram does not show how the board is being run, and a note like this one does. Each of the seven loads has a small lamp to its right that is lit when it has supply. Both AC boards here are three-phase, so on the AC side each line stands for a three-phase cable. On the DC side it stands for a DC pair. At phone width the sheet is drawn tall to fit. The sources sit in a row at the top, three feeders hang under each section, and the 115 V and DC boards sit beneath their sections. Tags are at least 12 px, and each device is a tap target about 40 px across. The rule. A line is live when an unbroken path of closed breakers and isolators joins it to a live source. The live sources are a running set, the shore supply with -Q3 closed, and the battery with -Q5 closed. Live lines are drawn bold in ink and dead lines pale. Power passes on through -T1 and -U1 to the boards below them. Tap any breaker or isolator to open or close it. Every line below it then redraws. The readout Loads with supply counts the lit lamps. Two cards keep the board honest. Closing a breaker that would join two live AC parts fed by different sources, such as -Q4 with both sets on, brings up a card: synchronise first. The breaker stays open. Charger -U1 and battery -G3 share the DC board in normal running. So -Q5 and -Q22 close freely. Closing -Q13 or -Q23 while the other is closed brings up a card: interlocked, open the other first. On the two Isolate screens, once an answer is checked, a Board or Isolate switch sits above the sheet. In Isolate mode you tap a load to choose it, then tap what you would lock off. Each device you tap opens and shows a padlock. A result card says one of three things about the chosen load. Live, naming a source and the path. Dead, but naming a device on a path that is not locked and could close. Or Isolated, when every path from every source, running or not, passes through a padlock. The readout Other loads taken off counts the other loads that lost supply, and lists them by tag in red. Choices stack one to a row at phone width, and the readouts and the switch wrap onto new lines, with no word split. Every tag stays readable at 360 px. Screen by screen. Screen 1, do, Still there?: the board as drawn, both sections live, -Q4 marked. "-G1 feeds section A and -G2 feeds section B. Can you close bus-tie -Q4 now?" Choices: Yes, both sections are at 440 V; Not until -G2 is synchronised with -G1 (right). Hint on Yes: "Matching voltage is not enough. Frequency and phase must match too." Why: closing -Q4 would join two running sets. Unless their voltage, frequency and phase match, a large current flows the moment it closes. So they are synchronised first. A right answer says "Still there." After Check, tapping -Q4 shows the synchronise first card. Screen 2, show, The power map: the whole board, lighting up in reading order. Words: "A single-line diagram maps a board's power, from each source through the busbars to each load. Read it in that order, sources first. The thick lines are the busbars. On the AC side, each line stands for all three phases of its cable. On the DC side, it stands for a pair of wires." The board stays as drawn. An amber glow traces the source lines in turn, then the two busbar sections, then each line down to its load. Read: an amber glow traces each line in that order, sources first. Still: the end of the sweep. Screen 3, do, typed, Count the sources: the board as drawn. "How many sources does this drawing show?" A typed answer: 4, a whole number. Slips: 3, "A source is anything that pushes power in. Look at the bottom of the sheet too."; 2, "Count the shore supply and the battery too. A source counts even with its breaker open."; 5, "-T1 and -U1 only pass power on from the main board. They are not sources." Hint: "Look for generator sets, the shore supply and any battery, anywhere on the sheet." Why: two generator sets and the shore supply sit at the top. Battery -G3 sits down on the DC board. -T1 and -U1 pass power on. So the drawing shows 4 sources. Loads with supply shows its real value here, 7 of 7. After Check, the four sources ring in ink. Screen 4, show, Live and dead: the board as drawn. Words: "Live lines are bold and dead lines pale. A breaker feeds everything below it, through every transformer and charger on the way." Then "Watch -Q1, the breaker of -G1, open. Tap it to close it again." Read: with -Q1 open, section A and everything below it are pale. Section B stays bold from -G2. Still: -Q1 open. Screen 5, do, typed, One breaker opens: the board as drawn, -Q12 marked. "Breaker -Q12 opens. How many loads lose supply?" A typed answer: 2, a whole number. Slips: 0, "-T1 is not a load. Follow its line on to the board it feeds."; 1, "The 115 V board feeds two loads. Count both."; 4, "Only what hangs below -Q12 goes. The rest of section A stays live." Hint: "Follow -Q12's line down through -T1 to each breaker below it." Why: -Q12 feeds transformer -T1. -T1 feeds the 115 V board. That board feeds lighting -E1 and fan -M4. So 2 loads lose supply, and the rest of section A stays live. Loads with supply shows ? until the answer is checked. After Check, -Q12 opens, its lines go pale, and Loads with supply reads 5. Screen 6, show, Where the voltage changes: the lower half of the sheet. Words: "A transformer marks where the voltage changes. Here -T1 steps 440 V down to 115 V. Charger -U1 turns 440 V AC into 24 V DC. Battery -G3 sits on the same DC board. On this sheet, a cross marks a breaker and a bar an isolator. Two circles are a transformer, and a box with ~ and = is a charger. The battery is drawn as long and short plates." Each board's voltage label lights in turn, then the battery. Screen 7, do, The charger's breaker: the board as drawn, -Q22 marked. "Breaker -Q22 opens. Is the 24 V DC board still live?" Choices: No, its only feed is open; Yes, from battery -G3 (right). Hint on No: "Find every source on that board, not only the feed from above." Why: opening -Q22 takes the charger off, so the main board no longer feeds the DC board. Battery -G3 is a source in its own right, joined through -Q5. So -E3 and -A3 stay lit, running on the battery. After Check, -Q22 opens, the charger's line goes pale and the DC board stays bold from -G3. Screen 8, show, The bus-tie: the board as drawn. Words: "Bus-tie -Q4 joins the two sections. It is marked N.O., for normally open. So each section runs on its own set. Close it and one set can feed both." Then "Watch -Q2 open and -Q4 close. With -Q2 open, section B is dead, so -Q4 can close without synchronising. Tap either one to try it yourself." Read: -Q2 is open and -Q4 is closed. -Q2 opened first. That left section B dead, so -Q4 could close without synchronising. Section B is bold again, fed from -G1 through the tie. Still: -Q2 open, -Q4 closed. Screen 9, do, Through the tie: both sets have stopped, -Q1 and -Q2 are open and -Q3 is closed, so the shore supply feeds section B and section A is pale. "Both sets have stopped, and -Q1 and -Q2 are open. Shore breaker -Q3 is closed, so the shore supply feeds section B. You close bus-tie -Q4. What feeds pump -M1 now?" Choices: Nothing, section A is dead; The shore supply, through the bus-tie (right); -G2, through the bus-tie. Hint on Nothing: "You have closed -Q4. Follow the line through it." Hint on -G2: "-G2 has stopped and -Q2 is open. Find the source that is still live." Why: -M1 hangs from section A. With -Q4 closed, section A joins section B, and the shore supply feeds both. A normally open breaker carries nothing across until it closes. Once closed, it carries power like any other. After Check, -Q4 closes and section A goes bold from the shore supply. Screen 10, show, Two ways in: the board as drawn, -M3 and its two feeds picked out. Words: "Pump -M3 is fed two ways. -Q13 feeds it from section A. -Q23, marked N.O., feeds it from section B. An interlock lets only one of them close at a time." Then "Watch -Q13 open and -Q23 close. Tap either one to try it yourself." Read: -Q13 is open and -Q23 is closed. -M3 is bold again, fed from section B. Still: -Q13 open, -Q23 closed. Screen 11, do, Lock it off: Isolate mode, with pump -M3 chosen and the board as drawn. "You must work on pump -M3 and keep every other load running. Each device you lock off gets a padlock. What do you lock off?" Choices: -Q13, its normal feed; -Q13 and -Q23 (right); -Q1 and -Q2, both sets' breakers. Hint on -Q13: "Opening -Q13 is what frees -Q23 to close. Lock off every way in." Hint on -Q1 and -Q2: "That takes off both sections. Shore breaker -Q3 could still close onto section B." Why: -M3 has two ways in. Opening -Q13 frees -Q23 to close, so both get a lock. Then every path from every source stops at a padlock. Nothing else loses supply. The drawing tells you what to lock off. Prove it dead at the pump before you start. After each Check, Isolate mode locks what was chosen and shows its result card and red list. Screen 12, do, mixed, typed, A set trips: the board as drawn. "Breaker -Q2 trips open. -Q3 and -Q4 stay open. How many loads lose supply?" A typed answer: 1, a whole number. Slips: 3, "Battery -G3 keeps the DC board live, so -E3 and -A3 stay lit."; 4, "Battery -G3 keeps the DC board live. -M3 runs on -Q13 from section A."; 2, "-M3 runs on -Q13 from section A. Its feed from section B is normally open." Hint: "Trace each load on section B back to a running source. Check the DC board and -M3." Why: section B goes dead, so pump -M2 stops. The charger stops too, but battery -G3 keeps -E3 and -A3 lit. -M3 runs from section A, and -Q23 is open. So 1 load loses supply. Loads with supply shows ? until the answer is checked, then 6. Screen 13, do, mixed, The alarm panel: Isolate mode, with alarm panel -A3 chosen and the board as drawn. "You must work on alarm panel -A3 and keep emergency lighting -E3 lit. What do you lock off?" Choices: -Q22, the charger's breaker; -Q22 and battery isolator -Q5; -F4, its own breaker (right). Hint on -Q22: "Battery -G3 still feeds the DC board. Look nearer -A3." Hint on -Q22 and -Q5: "-A3 is isolated, but -E3 goes dark too. Find the device nearest -A3." Why: -A3 has one way in from its board, through -F4. Lock off -F4, and every path to -A3 stops there, from the charger and from the battery. -E3 stays lit. After each Check, Isolate mode locks what was chosen, so a wrong choice shows -A3 still live, or -E3 listed in red.
interactive.ignores: Each line stands for a whole cable. The board has far fewer parts than a real one. A bold line means joined to a source. It does not show how much current flows. Nothing here trips. There are no overloads, fault currents or discrimination between breakers. One set can carry every load. The synchronise card stands for all of a real synchroniser's checks. Many boards interlock the shore breaker so it can never close onto a live section. A real transformer can pass power upward from a source on its lower side. The interlock between -Q13 and -Q23 is one simple kind. Real single-line diagrams also carry ratings, cable sizes and earthing. They are left off here. The battery never runs down. The voltages are example values for a board of this kind, not those of any real plant.

explain.text:
A single-line diagram is a board's power map. It outlines the connections from the power sources, through the switchboard and its busbars, to the loads that use the power. The sources can be generators, a shore supply and battery banks.[^2] So you read it from each source down to each load. Ask one question of every load. Which closed paths join it to a source?

The incoming power usually sits at the top. The drawing works its way down from there.[^3] On a three-phase system, one line stands for a bus or cable with all three of its phases.[^1] Each [[bus section]] is drawn here as a thick line. Every outgoing breaker hangs from it. A load has supply while an unbroken path of closed breakers joins it to a live source. Open a breaker and the path through it breaks. So everything below it loses supply, unless another path still reaches it. A path can pass through a transformer or a charger. Power passes on through them at a new voltage. On the example board, -T1 steps 440 V down to 115 V. Charger -U1 makes 24 V DC. Open -Q12 and both loads on the 115 V board lose supply. Nothing else does. Not every source sits at the top. The battery here sits on the DC board. So opening the charger's breaker leaves that board live.

This drawing marks two breakers N.O., for normally open. They stay open in normal running. One is the [[bus-tie]] -Q4, which joins the two bus sections. Kept open, it leaves each section on its own source. Close it and one source feeds both. A dead section then comes back live. If different sets keep both sections live, the sets must be synchronised before the tie closes. The other is -Q23, pump -M3's [[alternate feed]] from section B. Its normal feed is -Q13 from section A. An interlock lets only one of the two close. So opening -Q13 is exactly what lets -Q23 close. A normally open breaker carries nothing past it until it closes. Either side of it can still be live. Once closed, it carries power like any other. So to isolate a load, find every way in. Lock each one off, as near the load as you can. That way the loads that must keep running stay on.

**A load has supply while any path of closed breakers joins it to a source, so isolating it means finding every way in and locking each one off.**

analogy.text: You know this from a house with solar panels. The main switch takes the mains supply off. Yet the panels still make power whenever light falls on them. They are a second source. That is why you fit a dual supply warning at the board. A single-line diagram is that warning drawn out in full, for every source and every load.
analogy.breaks: A house usually has one main switch and one other source. Both are labelled at the board. A switchboard like this one has several sources. A bus-tie or alternate feed that is open today can be closed tomorrow. An up-to-date diagram is the one place that shows every way in.

practice.text:
- Isolate, lock off and prove dead at the point of work, as you always do. The diagram tells you where to isolate, never that a part is dead. A load may also have a control or heater supply that the single-line diagram does not show.
- Find every source first: generator sets, the shore supply and any battery, wherever they sit on the sheet.
- Find the busbars. Then follow each breaker down to everything it feeds, through every transformer and charger.
- Note every part marked normally open, such as a bus-tie or an alternate feed. Ask what it would feed the moment it closed.
- For the load you must work on, trace back up every path to every source. Each path is a way in.
- Lock off every way in, as near the load as you can. Then nothing else that must keep running goes dead.
- Check that each breaker on the board carries the tag the drawing gives it.
- On an insulated system, a closed tie joins two systems into one. An earth fault on either side is then a fault on both.

**Rule of thumb:** a load is isolated only when every path from every source stops at one of your locks.

**Worked example:** pump -M3 on the example board. Its normal feed is -Q13 from section A. Tracing up from the pump finds a second line, -Q23 from section B, marked normally open. An interlock lets -Q23 close once -Q13 opens. So lock off both -Q13 and -Q23. Every path from the sets and the shore supply now stops at a lock. No other load loses supply.

**Common mistakes**
- Locking off only the breaker the drawing names as the load's feed, and missing its alternate feed.
- Forgetting a bus-tie that is open now but can close.
- Starting at the top of the sheet and missing a battery drawn lower down.
- Taking a transformer or a charger as the end of the line. Power passes on through them.
- Opening a whole section or a set's breaker to kill one load. It takes off loads that must keep running. Another source can still close onto that section.
- Reading one line as one wire. On the AC side it stands for all three phases.

sources.title: us coast guard marine safety center plan review guideline
sources.quote: The purpose of an electrical one-line diagram is to provide an elementary schematic outlining connections from power sources (generators, shore power, battery banks) through a distribution system (switchboard, busbars, cables, feeders, and panels) to supply various power consuming loads.

sources.title: How to Read a Single Line Diagram | EECO
sources.quote: A one line typically starts at the top of the page and works its way down. It will start with the utility or other means of incoming power and its disconnecting device.

checks.label: A one-line diagram outlines the connections from the power sources (generators, shore power, battery banks) through the switchboard and busbars to the loads: here two generator sets, a shore supply and a battery feed the board, and each of the 7 loads has a path to a source

A one line starts at the top with the incoming power and its disconnecting device, then works its way down: the sets and the shore supply sit above their breakers, the breakers above the busbars, and every load lower still

Counted by hand: the drawing shows 4 sources (3 at the top, 2 sets, 5 counting -T1 and -U1); opening -Q12 takes off 2 loads (slips 0, 1 and 4), leaving 5 of 7; -Q2 tripping takes off 1 (slips 3, 4 and 2), leaving 6; the typed fields ask exactly these

Power passes on down through -T1 and -U1, never back up: with -Q22 open, battery -G3 keeps the DC board live while the charger's input stays dead; with -Q12 open the 115 V board is dead and section A stays live

Closing -Q4 as drawn would join -G1 and -G2, so the synchronise card comes up and -Q4 stays open; with -Q2 open it closes and -G1 feeds section B; -Q23 cannot close while -Q13 is closed; -Q5 and -Q22 close freely
On shore supply with both sets stopped, -Q4 closes without synchronising and the shore supply then feeds section A, so -M1 is fed through the bus-tie
Isolating -M3: -Q13 alone leaves -Q23 free to close from -G2; -Q13 and -Q23 isolate it with no other load taken off; -Q1 and -Q2 leave the shore supply a way in through -Q3 and take off 4 other loads
Isolating -A3: -Q22 alone leaves it live from battery -G3; -Q22 and -Q5 isolate it but take off -E3; -F4 alone isolates it and keeps -E3 lit
Before an answer nothing gives it away: every puzzle opens on its own board with nothing locked and no card, and both typed screens' readouts show ?
Every demonstration settles within 4.5 s of its screen opening, and every answer's motion within 2.5 s

applied.problem: The common mistake says opening a set's breaker or a whole section "works", but screen 11 shows it does not: another source, such as shore breaker -Q3 or the bus-tie, can still close onto that section. And a load can have control or heater supplies a single-line diagram leaves off.

"Its supply side stays live" is not always true: a bus-tie can be live on both sides, or on neither. "Goes dead" overstates what opening a breaker proves (the practice rightly says the diagram never shows a part is dead), and a bus section is not drawn thick on every sheet.

The synchronise rule fires for any two live parts fed by different sources, so re-closing -Q5 or -Q22 with the battery and charger both live would wrongly demand synchronising on DC, where they share the board in normal running. Screen 9's "supply side stays live" has the same fault as the explanat…

The model lets power pass only downward through -T1 and lets the shore supply be synchronised onto a live section; a real transformer can backfeed from a source on its lower side, and many boards interlock the shore breaker so it cannot close onto a live section at all.
